name: Wei Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does a normal workday look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on building sites, mostly framing walls, hanging doors and putting right work that did not fit the drawing. I have a vocational trade certificate and enough years on site to know when a timber is bowed, though I am no foreman. I use AI every day to draft a cut list or check the order before I send it, then measure the wall myself. My partner Iris and I have two school-age children, a mortgage and about three months of expenses saved. The pay is ordinary for the trade, and there are a few other contractors nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the lads a quicker cut list is fine if the tape measure still wins. A wall does not straighten itself because a screen drew it square.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My building work and pay would carry on, and three months saved gives our family room to breathe. I would keep using the tools I already know, with my hand on the timber before ordering more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my present site shifts and draft cut lists with the AI tool I use now. In the first year I would compare two lists with actual wall measurements before the timber order goes in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. The mortgage still needs feeding, but this picture does not take work from my hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which measurement catches a bad list?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A doorway can be ten millimetres narrower at the top than at the bottom. I would write both figures beside the list before cutting the frame.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a new tool for the job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. The existing company tool and my tape do the job, and Iris and I have other places for our money.

say: **Cut lists** can be quicker if actual wall measurements still decide.
**Timber work** remains physical despite tidy drawings.
think: My **site shifts and pay** remain steady under a plateau.
Our **three-month cushion** protects the mortgage against a short gap.
do: **Keep** current framing and door-fitting shifts while measuring each wall before cutting materials.
**Check** two AI cut lists against measured walls before ordering timber.
feel: **Calm**, while keeping the mortgage in mind.
S0.quote: A wall does not straighten itself because a screen drew it square.
fieldNote: He uses **AI daily** for cut lists but relies on a tape at the wall.
His **moderate savings** and continuing trade work support a calm mood.

steps.text: Keep site framing and door-fitting shifts with measured cut lists

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the buying desk and schedulers will feel AI before the workers fixing crooked frames. Robots spread onto sites more slowly, and I would want real job times before the programme is tightened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a scheduler cuts the allowance for fitting and repairs, I could lose paid hours on each job. We have three months saved and some nearby contractors, but a mortgage can eat that quickly if several payslips come in short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare a month of scheduled door jobs with actual fitting time and material delays. In the first year I would show the log to my site manager and put half of any extra weekend job pay into savings if such work comes in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a shorter paid week, though I would try a system that gave us the right materials on time. I cannot invoice a wall for being crooked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What delay would the schedule miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A door frame may arrive the wrong size and need a replacement before I can fit it. I would record the wait separately from the hands-on work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What weekend work could bring extra pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a neighbour books me to hang a door, I would take the job outside my site hours and put half that fee aside. I will not budget for it before anyone calls.

say: **Buying and scheduling** change before robots can handle the physical fitting and repair work on building sites.
**Real job times** must include wrong materials and repairs.
think: Tighter **paid hours** could leave several short payslips.
Three months saved and **some nearby jobs** offer only limited room.
do: **Log** a month of door jobs, fitting time and material delays.
**Take** a paid weekend door job if offered.
**Save** half of any earned weekend fee.
feel: **Anxious** about paid hours despite interest in better ordering.
S1.quote: I cannot invoice a wall for being crooked.
fieldNote: He sees **AI scheduling** as an income risk for a non-standard site job.
His **weekend work and saving** both depend on an actual booking and fee, not imagined earnings.

steps.text: Take paid weekend door-hanging job if neighbour books it
Save half of any earned weekend door-hanging fee

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that thinking AI can handle plans and orders by 2028, while capable building robots arrive about 2031. Three years of hands-on framing and fitting remain between those dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am good enough on site, but a robot that frames and hangs doors could reduce my shifts after 2031. We have three months saved and a mortgage, and the other contractors nearby may be buying the same machines; I cannot assume a quick move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the main contractor to let me trial robot layout software on a small room and learn its controls before it touches a live job. If paid training leads to a real local site-checking vacancy, I would take it; after 2028 I would apply for that post only at a wage that covers our mortgage and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with more work to do than time. I would rather know where a building robot puts a stud than wait for a new rota with my shifts missing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check in the trial room?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the robot’s marked stud positions with the actual floor and doorway measurements. A small offset can leave every board wrong by the far wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the site-checking post pays less?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Iris and I would compare the offer with the mortgage and school costs. If the wage ate our savings each month, I would keep looking for construction work instead.

say: **2028 thinking AI** reaches plans before capable building robots around 2031.
**Hands-on fitting** continues during the three-year gap.
think: Our **mortgage and three-month cushion** limit the time to find equal pay.
do: **Learn** robot layout controls in a small-room trial.
**Take** paid site-checking training only for a real local vacancy.
**Apply** after 2028 only if the wage covers mortgage and bills.
feel: **Anxious** about losing shifts, but able to start learning.
S2.quote: I would rather know where a building robot puts a stud than wait for a new rota with my shifts missing.
fieldNote: He looks for a **hands-on trial** that measures layouts against a real room.
His **training and application** require paid instruction, a genuine local post and bill-covering wages.

steps.text: Learn building robot layout controls in a small-room trial
Take paid site-checking training if linked to real local vacancy
Apply for local site-checking after 2028 only if pay covers mortgage and bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives us time to test a robot on uneven floors before thinking AI arrives in 2031. The field machines reach full hands-on ability around 2034, so I would expect a proper trial before changing the crew size.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By then my children will be older and the mortgage may still be heavy. I could build a small stream of repair jobs outside my site shifts, but I would not give up steady employment on the strength of a few enquiries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my current construction job and ask past customers for two paid weekend repair bookings this year. In the first year after 2031, if the bookings become regular enough to cover materials and tax, I would continue them while checking whether a local site-checking post pays at least our fixed bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wary, but five years lets me test a customer list before I rely on it. I do not want the children’s school costs riding on a maybe from weekend building repairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which repairs would you take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Small door and stair repairs that one person can finish safely on a weekend. I would price the material before promising a customer a date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How many bookings would make the side work useful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two paid jobs a month would be a start, after material costs. If it stayed at one enquiry and no deposit, I would keep it out of our budget.

say: **Uneven-floor trials** should precede capable building robots around 2034, before contractors change carpentry crew sizes.
**Crew size** should follow proven site results.
think: The **mortgage and school costs** may still need steady wages.
A small **repair sideline** could help only with real paid bookings.
do: **Seek** two paid weekend door or stair repair bookings.
**Continue** the side work after 2031 only if payments cover materials and tax.
feel: **Wary**, with time to test actual demand.
S3.quote: I do not want the children’s school costs riding on a maybe from weekend building repairs.
fieldNote: He tests **customer demand** without treating enquiries as earned income.
His **side work** stays beside the construction job unless paid bookings cover material and tax costs.

steps.text: Seek two paid weekend door or stair repair bookings
Keep construction shifts while testing paid side repairs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade puts thinking AI in 2036 and capable hands-on robots around 2039. I would use the time to pay down the mortgage and teach my children that a trade can change while you are still in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be in my fifties when the robots reach sites, with many working years potentially left. If my site work shrinks then, I would need more than a little repair sideline; ten years gives me room to build the savings first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep framing and fitting now and add a fixed amount from every paid weekend repair to the mortgage, if those repairs actually happen. In the first year after 2036 I would apply for local building inspection work only if a real opening offers pay that covers our bills and any required training is funded.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the far end, but not cornered. A decade lets me make the mortgage smaller before I decide whether to leave the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What fixed amount would you pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Iris and I would put fifty from each paid repair toward the mortgage after materials are covered. A month with no paid carpentry repair jobs would add nothing to our mortgage payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children learn the trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show them how to measure and fit a frame if they want to learn. I would not tell them carpentry is guaranteed work forever, even though it has fed our household.

say: **2036 thinking AI** comes before capable building robots around 2039.
**Trade skills** can change over a long working life.
think: Robot work might shrink **site shifts** in 2039.
Ten years lets us reduce **mortgage debt** if paid repairs come in.
do: **Keep** framing and fitting on the main site.
**Pay** fifty extra toward the mortgage from each paid repair after materials.
**Apply** for local inspection after 2036 only with funded training and bill-covering pay.
feel: **Anxious** about future shifts, with time to strengthen finances.
S4.quote: A month with no paid carpentry repair jobs would add nothing to our mortgage payment.
fieldNote: His **extra debt payment** comes only from paid repairs after materials.
His **inspection move** depends on a real local opening, funded training and bill-covering wages.

steps.text: Keep framing and fitting on current site
Pay fifty extra on mortgage per paid repair after materials
Apply for local building inspection after 2036 only with funded training and bill-covering pay

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because capable building robots around 2031 could cut paid framing shifts while the mortgage and school bills are still large. Paid site-checking training tied to a local job would help more than a brochure.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask what happens when the robot measures a wall that was never straight. I want the person with the tape to have the final word before any studs are cut.

portrait: **Wei Jensen**, 43, is an experienced construction worker with a vocational trade certificate who frames walls and fits doors.
He and partner Iris have **two school-age children**, a mortgage, typical trade pay and about three months of expenses saved.
He uses **AI daily** for cut lists and is keen to test building robot layout on a real room.
A **traditional work ethic** leads him toward paid weekend repair jobs and paying down mortgage debt from actual fees.
The **2028 scenario** worries him most because capable robots could reduce site shifts while family bills remain high.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut framing shifts around 2031 before he has enough savings to protect mortgage and school costs.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **site-checking training** tied to a local job at bill-covering pay would give him another wage path.
headlineQuote: I want the person with the tape to have the final word before any studs are cut.
